findings.title: limitFunction drops all caller arguments before invoking the wrapped function
findings.cause: The wrapper returned at index.js:124 is `return () => limit(() => function_());`, so it accepts no rest parameters and always calls the original function with zero arguments. The previous implementation in HEAD forwarded `(...arguments_)` into `function_(...arguments_)`.
findings.impact: Any use of `limitFunction()` with parameterized work receives `undefined` instead of the caller-provided values. The documented recipe `urls.map(url => limitedFetchUrl(url))` will call `fetchUrl()` without the URL, breaking real consumers while TypeScript still advertises argument forwarding.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:121-124 ignores arguments. index.d.ts:133-136 returns `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`. recipes.md:161-163 calls `limitedFetchUrl(url)`. Focused runtime probe printed `{"expected":"sentinel","actual":"ARG_WAS_UNDEFINED"}`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run the no-write probe: load index.js with an in-memory Queue shim, then `const limited = limitFunction(async value => value ?? "ARG_WAS_UNDEFINED", {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited("sentinel"));`. Actual: `ARG_WAS_UNDEFINED`; expected: `sentinel`.

findings.title: limit.map passes undefined index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call at index.js:108-112 gates index forwarding on `Array.isArray(iterable)`, so supported iterables like Set and array iterators receive `undefined` for the second argument.
findings.impact: The public contract says every mapper receives `(item, index)`. Consumers using indexes with Sets, generators, or iterators get undefined/NaN-derived results even though those iterable inputs are explicitly supported by tests and types.
findings.evidence: readme.md:78-84 and index.d.ts:30-43 say the mapper receives value and index for an `Iterable<Input>`. test.js:239-253 covers Set and array iterators but does not assert index. Focused probe printed `map_set_index: ["a:undefined","b:undefined"]` and `map_array_iterator_index: ["x:undefined","y:undefined"]`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `const limit = pLimit(2); await limit.map(new Set(["a", "b"]), (value, index) => `${value}:${index}`)`. Actual: `["a:undefined","b:undefined"]`; expected equivalent to Array.from semantics: `["a:0","b:1"]`.

findings.title: Options-object construction flips rejectOnClear default to true
findings.cause: The options destructuring at index.js:6-8 uses `rejectOnClear = true`, contradicting the documented and typed default of false.
findings.impact: `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` now rejects queued promises with AbortError when `clearQueue()` is called, even though users did not opt in. This can unexpectedly reject `Promise.all` chains in shutdown paths that previously left discarded tasks pending by default.
findings.evidence: readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 state `rejectOnClear` default is false. The readme itself shows `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` at readme.md:54-58. Focused probe printed `default_rejectOnClear_options: {"status":"rejected","name":"AbortError","message":"This operation was aborted"}`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run with an in-memory Queue shim: create `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1});` queue one long task and one pending task, call `limit.clearQueue()`, then race the pending promise against a timeout. Actual: rejected AbortError; expected under documented default false: still pending/discarded without rejection.

findings.title: Falsey non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation at index.js:12 only throws when `rejectOnClear` is truthy and non-boolean, so values like 0, empty string, or null are accepted even though the option is documented as boolean.
findings.impact: Invalid configuration can silently change behavior instead of failing fast. This weakens the runtime contract and diverges from the existing tsd expectation that non-boolean rejectOnClear values are errors.
findings.evidence: index.d.ts:99-106 declares `rejectOnClear?: boolean`; index.test-d.ts:29 expects an error for a string non-boolean. Current validation skips falsey non-booleans. Focused probe printed `rejectOnClear_zero_validation: {"threw":false}`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})`. Actual: no throw; expected: TypeError matching the boolean-only option contract.

findings.title: Infinity concurrency is rejected despite prior implementation support
findings.cause: The validator at index.js:127-129 now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)`, removing the previous explicit `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance visible in `git show HEAD:index.js` lines 123-126.
findings.impact: Callers that used `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)` as an unlimited/pass-through mode now get a TypeError. This is an edge-case behavioral regression in the package API surface.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:127-129 rejects non-integers. Baseline `git show HEAD:index.js` line 124 allowed `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`. Focused probe printed `concurrency_infinity: {"accepted":false,"name":"TypeError","message":"Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up"}`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)`. Actual: TypeError. Expected from prior source behavior: accepted as a valid concurrency value.
